title: Goodnight Stories | Notes on an Aria Exercise
subtitle: Written after A Withering Aria: an exercise in the structure of remembering and not remembering
body:
Creating is like conducting, and this afterword is like the rehearsal room the audience never sees.

This story did not begin as a “finished conception.” It came from Teacher Qingdou’s writing-training plan, whose prompt required a fixed opening sentence:

“I cannot remember names, people’s faces, or what cars look like.”

At first I tried several directions and could not continue any of them. Until one day, I thought of a sentence:

“I was lying. Actually, I can remember.”

It was a gentle counterattack, and an intensely private confession. Suddenly I realized that perhaps I did not need to construct the plot starting from “loss.” I only needed to place someone amid all this floating and loosening, and let her slowly find that little bit of “what she still remembers.”

So I had the story’s two endpoints: the loss of speech at the beginning, and the affirmation at the end. Everything between them was how to make that sentence hold true.

## Someone Who Has Lost “Hearing” Still Lives in Rhythm

The protagonist has not truly lost her hearing. What she has lost is the ability to distinguish “pitch,” progressing from disordered absolute pitch to an inability to judge even relative pitch. This is an extremely hidden yet despairing collapse of hearing. It means she can no longer play the violin.

I wanted her to be a former genius violinist. Not for dramatic effect, but because only when a “heightened capacity for perception” is stripped away can the story’s pain take deeper root. She has not lost sound; she has lost her way of perceiving the world’s order. She can still hear waves, voices, the roar of machinery, but everything has lost its internal relationships, leaving only corroded echoes in warm water.

She can no longer continue living on land. In a world of noise and speed, she has lost direction. So she chooses to board a ship and play jazz on a cruise liner, accompanying people who are drinking.

Why jazz? Because jazz is what she can still control. Rhythm and floating points, improvisation and instability: these are the areas her remaining perception can contend with. She no longer touches classical music. She is unwilling to confront melodies once so familiar and now impossible to recognize.

## The One Who Understood Goldberg
Someone understood her playing. Within that improvised jazz, she heard a faint flavor of the Goldberg Variations. She did not approach and say, “You play very well.” She only ordered a cocktail called “Aria Morta” and left a note.

This tentative approach is a very delicate emotional arrangement. It is neither a confession nor a tease, but a “recognition” of the protagonist’s most hidden part.

At first the protagonist feels she has been flirted with. She has always been extremely restrained: she does not drink, does not express too much, does not respond casually. She neither removes the drink nor drinks it, but places it on the piano. This is her hesitation, and also a silent assent. She does not want to open the door to her emotions, but she has not rejected the other person’s approach either.

I wrote this scene because I wanted to capture an emotional rhythm not often written about: not ardent admiration, but a perceptive resonance between performers. An approach that says, “I have understood you, but I will not disturb you.”

## Dreams Are Her Hearing the Other’s Practice
Over the next few nights, she begins to dream.

Sometimes the ceiling begins to seep water, like the fine, low-pitched vibration of a bass string;

sometimes vines grow wildly, winding around mirror and memory together;

sometimes blue butterflies pour through the window, settle on her fingertips, and tremble slightly.

These dreams are not fantasies. She is using her remaining perception of rhythm to catch another person’s daily practice. The other is a violinist preparing for a performance, practicing three violin concertos each day. The protagonist cannot distinguish the melodies, but the strange visions in her dreams tell her the answer.

I wanted these dreams to be more than “visualized” fragments: a nonverbal auditory echo. For her, this is the only way still connecting her to the world. She cannot find the other’s face, but she can recognize that set of rhythms, that manner of playing—the “breath” she once knew.

## Answering Love with Performance Instead of Language
I arranged for her to stop playing jazz at her final-night performance on the ship and return to those three classical violin concertos.
She knows the audience will not like this performance, and knows she may not play accurately. Yet she still chooses to play, because this is a letter, a confession.

I also arranged for her to reverse the sections of *The Butterfly Lovers*: beginning with “Transformation into Butterflies,” skipping “Farewell,” and ending with “Meeting.”
I did not want the whole piece to end in the high notes of “wings broken, music ended.” I wanted her final love to rest on the first gaze.

This is not a technical reconstruction, but an emotional arrangement. I wanted to put “first meeting” in the place of “goodbye,” to let love arrive rather than end.

## Giving Away the Violin, and the Heart
After the performance, she gives the other woman her own violin, a Stradivarius.
She does not say, “This is for you,” but, “I believe it will like living with you.”

This violin is her past, her heart, and the vessel of all her emotions.

Giving it away is the final chapter of her performing career.
It is also the most restrained, most sincere confession she can offer.

## An Invitation of Love: Performance Instead of Confession
She says, “Come to my performance.”
The other responds too. This time she neither sends a drink nor writes a note, leaving only a sentence before disembarking:

“Come to my performance.”

She does not say “I love you,” nor “Would you like to come?” She only leaves an invitation.

This is her way of confessing: if you come, perhaps we can have a future.

And she does not answer. She only drinks the glass that had first been left on the piano.

Silence is a refusal of the future in which they leave together.
Drinking acknowledges her love, and expresses a willingness to sink into it.

## About the Name
Her name is never spoken until the end.

On the day the ship docks, she plays Goldberg’s Aria da capo alone. Returning to the first melody, like the story making a full circle and finally arriving quietly at its beginning.

She closes her eyes and, in the spaces between the notes, sees her walking out of the light, wearing that night’s moonlight-gray dress.

Then she softly calls a name:

“Hahn.”

The name comes from my favorite performer, Hilary Hahn.
Her restraint, precision, gentleness, and depth are everything I wanted to write into both characters.

She is the one who hears Goldberg, and also the reflection of the former genius violinist.

I did not arrange for them to be together. Not because they “cannot,” but because:

Some love is already complete at the moment it is expressed.
It needs neither an answer nor a continuation.
It simply existed, becoming true when one person remembers another’s name.

## About the Story’s Structure and Title
The word “aria” itself carries a profound historical and emotional texture. It is not merely “singing a melody,” but “the moment of a character’s most essential emotional monologue” in a musical or opera.
In opera, Aria contrasts with Recitativo (recitative). Recitativo is dialogue that advances the plot, while Aria pauses to enter the echo chamber of a character’s inner emotions. An aria is therefore a suspended emotional space: the plot stops, the protagonist stands there, and sings what cannot be said. Like my protagonist, sitting in the empty cruise-ship bar after everyone has disembarked, playing Aria da capo as though speaking to herself: “Hahn.”

It usually has an A–B–A ternary structure, especially the “da capo aria” common in the Baroque period: A, B, then back to A. A is the first appearance of the emotion; B is struggle, reversal, or contrast; on returning to A, the emotion is already different—the melody is the same, but the feeling has changed. I used the same structure in this story. A: I do not remember, I float, I have lost. B: I meet her, she understands me, I give away the violin. Back to A (Aria da capo): I play alone, speak the name: “So I could remember, after all.”

In opera, whenever a character’s fate turns, whenever fate forces them into the deepest place, there is an aria. It is like an argument with fate, an acceptance of fate, despair, or longing—none of it reasonable, all of it real. In my story, this aria is not a roaring confession, but a melody about to wither, still singing softly; one person’s final performance of the melody she still remembers; a song of passage from “I forgot” to “I remember.”

Aria Morta, before all sounds began, this is how I once thought of you.
